title: THE FALL OF NVIDIA'S KING: How Jensen Huang Lost the Company He Built
description: An evidence-led English-language corporate crisis documentary about Jensen Huang's resignation, NVIDIA's board decision not to reinstate him, export-control scrutiny, national-security questions, governance and succession. scenes.title: THE FOUNDER IS GONE
scenes.subtitle: NVIDIA • NOVEMBER 2026
scenes.narration: For more than three decades, Jensen Huang was the public face of NVIDIA. The black leather jacket. The packed keynote arenas. The green logo. And behind that carefully recognizable image, a company that became one of the most important suppliers in the artificial intelligence economy. Its processors power data centers, train advanced models, and sit inside the infrastructure that technology companies are racing to build. Then, in November twenty twenty-six, NVIDIA announced that Huang had resigned as its president and chief executive officer, effective immediately. The board appointed its longtime finance chief, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. Five days later, the board delivered a second message: it did not intend to bring Huang back. This was not a routine retirement, and it was not simply a change of title. It was a sudden break between one of the most recognizable founders in technology and the company he had led since its creation. The story raises a much larger question. When a founder becomes inseparable from a corporation, who has the power to decide when the relationship is over? And can the company keep moving when the person who defined its identity is no longer in charge? The departure also forces a question about the relationship between a founder's personal authority and the formal structure of a listed company. Employees may associate the mission with the founder. Customers may trust the roadmap because they trust the person presenting it. Investors may see continuity and risk through the same individual. But directors are responsible for the company as a whole, including its controls, disclosures and long-term resilience. A board that acts in a crisis has to explain not only why it acted, but how the company will function afterward.

scenes.title: THE OFFICIAL BREAK
scenes.subtitle: A resignation accepted by the board
scenes.narration: The formal record is unusually direct. In a filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, NVIDIA said its board had accepted Huang's resignation as president, chief executive officer and a member of the board, effective immediately. The filing identifies November eleventh as the date of the board action. The company announced the transition publicly the following day. Colette Kress, NVIDIA's executive vice president and chief financial officer, was appointed interim chief executive while directors began a search for a permanent successor. Kress had been the company's finance chief since twenty thirteen. The board also appointed Harvey C. Jones as its chair. These details matter because they establish what actually happened, rather than what headlines or social media might imply. NVIDIA described the departure as a resignation. The board accepted it. The public filing does not describe a formal dismissal. But the distinction between a resignation and a board-approved exit does not make the transition ordinary. The timing, the speed of the announcement, and the board's later refusal to reinstate Huang show that directors were prepared to assert authority over the founder. For a company whose public identity had been built around one person, this was a defining governance moment. A leadership transition at this scale is also a communications test. Customers make multi-year infrastructure decisions. Cloud companies plan capacity years ahead. Developers build software around hardware and software platforms that they expect to support for a long time. Any perception of instability can become a business issue even when factories continue shipping and engineers keep working. That is why the interim CEO's first task is not simply to occupy the office. It is to show customers and partners that commitments, engineering priorities and support systems remain intact.

scenes.title: THE CRISIS BEHIND THE HEADLINES
scenes.subtitle: What is documented — and what remains unproven
scenes.narration: The resignation followed a week of intense scrutiny over Huang's personal conduct and media reports involving a woman described as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Those descriptions require care. A reported suspicion is not proof of espionage. An allegation is not a finding that classified information was transferred. And a corporate investigation is not a criminal conviction. NVIDIA's board said it was initiating an independent investigation after recent reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. In the same statement, the board said it had no reason to believe that national security or NVIDIA secrets had been compromised. Huang separately acknowledged serious mistakes in his personal life. The company has not publicly established that an intelligence operation succeeded, or that company information was improperly disclosed. The central fact is narrower, but still consequential: the board opened an investigation, the CEO resigned, and NVIDIA entered a leadership transition. That is enough to make this a major corporate story without presenting unproven claims as fact. A responsible account must keep three categories separate: what the company has formally disclosed, what journalists have reported, and what investigators have yet to establish. When the stakes involve a global technology supplier and national security, precision is not a technicality. It is the difference between reporting and speculation. The national-security issue is especially difficult because the public often sees only fragments: a reported relationship, a government concern, a company statement and a board investigation. None of those fragments alone answers the central questions. Investigators need evidence about access, intent, communications, controls and any actual transfer of protected information. Until that evidence is made public, a documentary should resist the temptation to connect every reported detail into a single definitive explanation. The chronology is clear; the full causal account is not.

scenes.title: WHY THE CHIPS MATTER
scenes.subtitle: A commercial product with strategic consequences
scenes.narration: To understand why this crisis reaches beyond the private life of one executive, look at what NVIDIA sells. Its advanced processors are central to the infrastructure used to train and run powerful artificial intelligence systems. They are among the most valuable components in the technology supply chain. That makes them commercial products, but also strategic assets. The United States has imposed export controls to restrict China's access to certain advanced computing chips. The policy is intended to limit the ability of foreign military and intelligence organizations to obtain computing power that could have national-security consequences. For NVIDIA, the rules create a difficult business environment. China is a major technology market, but the company must comply with restrictions on what products can be sold, to whom, and under what conditions. The questions now facing lawmakers are not abstract. How are end users verified? How do suppliers monitor intermediaries? What happens when a product is diverted after it leaves an authorized channel? And what responsibility does a chip designer have when its technology moves through a global network of distributors and cloud providers? These questions are bigger than one CEO. They go to the operating model of the entire advanced semiconductor industry. They also explain why a leadership crisis at NVIDIA quickly became a matter of national policy. Export controls are also hard to enforce because advanced computing products move through complex commercial networks. A chip can be sold to an approved customer, integrated into a server, rented through a cloud service or transferred through intermediaries. Regulators therefore examine more than the first invoice. They look at end users, beneficial ownership, product specifications, licensing, monitoring and the ability to detect diversion. The rules can change, and companies must adapt their compliance systems as products and customer structures evolve.

scenes.title: WASHINGTON WANTS ANSWERS
scenes.subtitle: Congressional scrutiny moves to the next stage
scenes.narration: The political response has moved beyond public statements. House committees announced that Huang had agreed to appear for a transcribed interview on December first. NVIDIA general counsel Tim Teter was scheduled to appear the following day. The committee chairmen said they wanted answers about the company's role in a potential breach of national security, including whether advanced chips reached restricted actors and what role a suspected intelligence asset may have played. Those are the lawmakers' stated concerns. They are not findings of wrongdoing. The interviews matter because they could clarify what the company knew, what controls it operated, and how officials assess the risk of diversion. Separately, reporting has described investigative scrutiny by California authorities concerning chip transfers and possible disclosures. The exact scope and outcome of those inquiries must be checked against official documents as they develop. For NVIDIA, the consequences may extend well beyond the CEO search. The company could face tougher compliance requirements, closer scrutiny of its sales channels, and new questions from customers and investors. For Washington, the case tests whether export controls can keep pace with a market where products are valuable, portable, and in extraordinary demand. The next stage is not a social-media argument. It is evidence, testimony and official findings. A congressional interview is not the same as a public trial. Transcribed testimony can help lawmakers build a record, test statements and decide whether legislation or further oversight is needed. It may also remain partly confidential. The public should not assume that a scheduled interview will produce immediate answers, or that the absence of a public finding proves that no risk existed. The important measure will be what evidence emerges and whether it is independently tested.

scenes.title: THE RETURN THAT DID NOT HAPPEN
scenes.subtitle: The board draws a line
scenes.narration: After leaving, Huang made clear that he was willing to return. He said he had heard calls from employees, investors, business partners and customers, and that he would be honored to come back if the board decided it was in the best interests of the company and its shareholders. The response from the board was equally clear. Chairman Harvey Jones said directors had unanimously accepted the resignation and did not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO. That statement transformed the story. A resignation can sometimes be followed by a negotiated return. Here, the board publicly closed that door, at least under its stated position at the time. The episode also produced a wave of online campaigning. But not everything circulating was genuine. Reuters Fact Check examined a viral image that purported to show hundreds of employees demanding that the board resign. It found the image was fabricated. A separate open letter asking the board to give Huang a fair hearing was real. Those are not the same thing. In a crisis around a public company, false claims can distort the apparent mood inside the workforce, mislead investors, and turn a complicated governance dispute into a simple internet spectacle. The verified record is more revealing: Huang offered to return, the board said no, and the company began planning for a future without him at the top. For investors, the founder's departure creates several separate questions. Will customers continue to commit to the same product roadmap? Can the company retain senior technical leaders? Will compliance changes affect which markets it can serve? And will the board's process restore confidence or create a longer period of uncertainty? A share price on one day cannot answer those questions. The business has to be judged through orders, deliveries, margins, customer concentration, product execution and the quality of its controls over time.

scenes.title: THE COMPANY BENEATH THE FOUNDER
scenes.subtitle: Can NVIDIA execute without its defining figure?
scenes.narration: The next challenge is operational. NVIDIA must reassure customers that product roadmaps will continue, reassure investors that execution will not falter, and demonstrate that governance and compliance systems can withstand scrutiny. Colette Kress knows the company's finances and operations after more than a decade as chief financial officer. But taking over during a crisis is different from managing a normal succession. The board must identify a permanent leader while the company answers questions from lawmakers and regulators. The business itself remains enormous. NVIDIA's latest quarterly results show that demand for its computing infrastructure has not simply disappeared with its founder's departure. Its data-center business has become a central engine of the company's growth. Before this film is locked, the exact figures from the official third-quarter fiscal twenty twenty-seven earnings release must be inserted with the reporting period and source shown on screen. The key point is not a single revenue number. It is that NVIDIA is an ecosystem: software developers, cloud providers, chip designers, manufacturing partners, networking suppliers and customers. That ecosystem cannot be moved by a single executive. But leadership matters when decisions involve billions of dollars, long product cycles, geopolitical risk and intense competition. The real test for Kress and the board is whether the company's systems are strong enough to preserve momentum while restoring confidence in its oversight. The succession question also reaches into the company's culture. NVIDIA's public image has long been tied to Huang's energy and technical storytelling. A successor may choose a different style, and that does not automatically mean a weaker company. In mature organizations, the real measure of leadership is whether talent can make decisions, whether risks are escalated, and whether the institution can correct mistakes. A successful transition would make the company less dependent on any one personality while preserving the engineering culture that customers value.

scenes.title: WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
scenes.subtitle: A test of leadership — and of the institution
scenes.narration: The next milestones are concrete. The board must choose a permanent chief executive. Investigators must establish what happened, and what did not. Congressional committees are scheduled to hear from Huang and NVIDIA's general counsel. The company must show that its export-control and compliance processes are credible. And investors will be watching whether customers, suppliers and developers continue to trust the company's roadmap. There is a deeper question for the technology industry. NVIDIA became one of the defining companies of the artificial-intelligence era under a founder whose personality became part of its brand. But a public company cannot depend on charisma alone. It needs durable systems, accountable leadership, independent oversight and controls that work even when the stakes are high. Huang built NVIDIA into an institution with global influence. Now that institution faces a test of its own. This is not the end of NVIDIA, and it is not proof that the company has lost its technological advantage. It is a moment when the world's attention has shifted from the products on stage to the decisions inside the boardroom. The question is no longer only whether NVIDIA can succeed without its founder standing at the keynote podium. It is whether the company can convince the world that its governance is as powerful as its technology.
